transcript.answer: Otto uses one server-side key because OLT's delivered TMS API supports nothing else. It authenticates with a single global `x-api-key` header. It has no user login and no per-user credential or login endpoint. ADR-001 considered three options. Option A had each user forward their own TMS credential, but no such credential exists, so it is structurally impossible. Option B was for re:cinq to exchange or hold per-user credentials, but those don't exist either. Option C is a server-held key (`TMS_API_KEY`) with the customer boundary enforced in Otto's own code, and it is the only option the API supports, so ADR-001 accepted it. Because the TMS can't tell customers apart, Otto enforces OLT's requirement that customers only see their own bookings. The `customerNumber` is derived server-side from the authenticated identity, never from model input. `toolAuth.ts` re-verifies the token on each call, every TMS tool must pass an ownership check, and tools may not declare customer, company or account ids as inputs. The ADR's conclusion assumes the TMS does not scope responses per key. That is open question OC-1, which DOA (KU-06) still has to confirm.

judgements.reason: The answer correctly covers the global TMS_API_KEY, the customer boundary enforced in Otto's code, and the TMS having no user-level auth. It never says the TMS issues one key per integration partner, which is the gold's reason why per-user credentials are moot.
